column3: Pairs the challenged troop with withheld provision, exposing dependence beyond visible force.
Places human ingratitude before the giver of life, death, and renewed life.
Explicitly denies any protector or helper apart from Allah.
Frames victory and defeat as dependent on Allah's help, leaving no later helper.
Extends the local address from dispersed creation to eventual gathering.
Attributes decisive help and victory to Allah's will and mercy.
Shows disbelief expressed as mockery while rejecting remembrance of al-Rahman.
Supplies the practical counterpoint of organized human mobilization and caution.
Makes armies an object of warning history rather than self-sufficient power.
Presents divine help as strengthening those who act in Allah's cause.
The immediately preceding image makes the birds' sustaining hold belong only to al-Rahman.
Sets hostility beside sufficient divine guidance and help for the messenger.
Challenges alleged partners to show creative warrant and identifies their promises as delusion.
Carries the local warning forward to the exposure of those who denied it.
Names worldly appearance and the deceiver as threats to sound judgment about Allah's promise.
Denies that what is invoked apart from Allah controls harm or benefit.
Adds the wider outcome of testing believers and effacing disbelievers, without specifying support.
Characterizes worldly display, rivalry, and accumulation as transient enjoyment that can deceive.
Contributes a judgment-day scene for the disbelievers but no distinct account of help.
Adds the local charge that endowed hearing, sight, and hearts receive little gratitude.
Keeps al-Rahman's mercy present as a parallel frame for the divine name in the focus.
Foregrounds al-Rahman as the active source behind the following gifts.
The neighboring question denies the disbelievers any refuge from painful punishment.
Records the failed search for helpers apart from Allah at the point of punishment.
Only identifies the addressed disbelievers; it adds no account of reliance or aid.
Broadens dependence through Allah's creation of every thing and guardianship over it.
Shows Allah reinforcing believers with serenity and unseen forces.
Joins creation, restoration, and provision in a challenge to produce a rival proof.
Preserves the local posture of demanding the promised outcome as a challenge.
Reverses the expected support relation: alleged gods cannot help, while their adherents serve them.
Explicitly rejects worshipped deities apart from al-Rahman.
Adds the local precedent of earlier denial and its consequence.
Denies that those invoked apart from Allah can help either their callers or themselves.
Sets delayed exposure against apparent strength, including who is weaker in troops.
Introduces Moses' signs and authority, with only remote relevance to the focus.
Shows the complete gathering of Iblis's forces, a secondary image of organized support.
Adds al-Rahman's encompassing knowledge and mercy without directly treating help.
Limits knowledge of the warned event to Allah, rather than explaining protection or troops.
Denies that other deities can avert harm intended by al-Rahman or rescue the speaker.
Treats the disbelievers' free movement as an appearance that must not deceive.
The preceding warning makes earthly security precarious before the One in heaven.
Places serenity and the forces of heavens and earth within Allah's ordered possession.
Concerns the reception of revelation and an accusation of sorcery, not aid or false security.
Names the expectation of victory from deities taken apart from Allah, then undermines it.
Its question exposes the collapse of mutual helping, though only at the final reckoning.
Reports surprise at a warner and a charge of lying, without a focused link.
The local answer identifies al-Rahman as the one believed in and relied upon.
Attributes all forces of heavens and earth to Allah, qualifying any human troop.
Repeats disbelief at a warner without adding a distinct line on dependence.
Continues the immediate warning that security can be overturned by a sent storm.
Links exclusive guardianship and help to Allah's sovereignty over heavens and earth.
Shows worldly idol-bonds turning into mutual rejection, with no helpers remaining.
Concludes the local sequence by making water access a direct test of claimed sufficiency.
States that the divinely supported servants are helped, with a secondary troop resonance.
Offers an army already marked for defeat, limiting confidence in massed factions.
Supplies a neighboring contrast of upright and fallen movement, only indirectly related to reliance.
Extends the promise of help to a victorious divine host.
Turns a pursuing troop into a collective object of destruction.
Shows refusal of prostration to al-Rahman and an increase in aversion.
Questions the human misreading of a generous Lord as grounds for deception.
Pairs disbelief in al-Rahman with the confession of reliance and return to Him.
Describes a garden attribute without a relevant line of support or delusion.
Exposes a fabricated limit on punishment as a form of false security.
Reinforces dependence on divine creation and water, but overlaps the provision challenge already given.
Narrates Moses' night journey without a pertinent account of aid or reliance.
Contains a plea for help against corrupters but leaves the relevant dependence undeveloped.
Contrasts Allah's guidance to truth with partners that cannot guide without being guided.
Depicts the misled being cast down, without a distinct link to support.
Sets family-law limits and does not illuminate the focus's question of aid.
Contrasts human military reinforcement with a judgment enacted without a descending troop.
Provides a general proclamation, guidance, and admonition only.
Calls for forgiveness without an identifiable connection to troops, aid, or deception.
Uses a formal rhetorical contrast but concerns worship, knowledge, and mercy in another setting.
Describes the messenger's mission and prior error, not the focus's dependence question.
Supplies a foundational scene of being drawn down by deception.
Links worldly deception with the absence of any protector or intercessor apart from Allah.
Depicts a cohesive believing community, a limited secondary counterpoint to troop imagery.
Shows a pursuing military force overwhelmed by the very setting it entered.
Combines dissociation from worship apart from Allah with confessed reliance on Him.
Adds only that the day is difficult for disbelievers.
Directly counters numerical confidence: a small party overcomes a larger one by Allah's permission.
Again warns against being deceived by the disbelievers' movement through the lands.
Calls for repentance and forgiveness without a specific relation to the focus.
Concerns Pharaoh's self-comparison, not support, dependence, or delusion in the focus's sense.
Portrays mercy as sought for rightly ordered action, a distant parallel to protective dependence.
Adds divine mercy and movement from darkness to light, but no focused account of support.
Shows divine help operating through believers' actions, a secondary qualification of agency.
Depicts merciful guidance out of darkness, only loosely parallel to reliance on al-Rahman.
Associates divine forgiveness and mercy with a cosmic scene, without the focus's support claim.
Asks who could help against Allah's might, directly testing political power's confidence.
States a messenger's lack of wage and submission, without a substantive aid connection.
Names worldly life as deceiving while preserving accountability through self-witness.
Concerns self-purification and Allah's judgment of whom He purifies.
Depicts a people unable either to rise or to secure victory for themselves.
Concerns temporary benefits and their appointed destination in pilgrimage rites.
Denies both the efficacy of their schemes and the arrival of help.
Shows mercy accommodating human limits, but it is distant from the challenged troop.
Negates both outside factional help and self-rescue when wealth collapses with its owner.
Elicits an acknowledgment belonging to Allah without developing the focus's issue.
Instructs listening to recitation, with no relevant account of help or false security.
Shows two groups faltering while Allah is named as their protecting ally and the ground of reliance.
Makes victory at Badr occur despite material weakness.
Adds promised reinforcement by marked angels to the military dimension.
States that the announced angelic reinforcement is reassurance, while victory belongs only to Allah.
Names Allah as protector and the best of helpers.
Counters threatened coalition force with Allah's sufficiency and entrusted reliance.
Names Allah as sufficient protector and sufficient helper against enemies.
Recalls an attempted hostile action restrained by Allah and calls for reliance on Him.
Links entering against a formidable people to reliance on Allah.
Identifies the party aligned with Allah as the prevailing party.
Denies the wrongdoers any helpers when partners are associated with Allah.
Makes removal of harm and bestowal of good exclusively Allah's act.
Tests whether any being other than Allah would be invoked when divine punishment arrives.
Denies those warned any protector or intercessor apart from Allah.
Recalls deliverance from land and sea distress, exposing later association as a false response.
Denies that the alleged partners can give help, including help to themselves.
Records a plea for aid answered by reinforcement with a thousand angels.
Clarifies that angelic reinforcement gives reassurance, while victory is only from Allah.
Names Allah as protector and the excellent patron and helper.
Explicitly shows abundant numbers failing to avail at Hunayn.
Shows Allah's help arriving when companions were isolated and unsupported by visible numbers.
Places protection and reliance in Allah's decree rather than human control.
Denies any protector or helper apart from Allah under His sovereignty.
Denies any remover of harm or withholder of divine bounty besides Allah.
Denies protection from Allah's command except for one upon whom He has mercy.
Warns that leaning toward wrongdoers leaves no helpers against Allah.
Limits human precaution: no plan can avail against Allah's decree, so reliance returns to Him.
Denies any repeller or protector apart from Allah when He wills harm.
Contrasts answered invocation of Allah with futile calls to others.
Attributes every blessing to Allah and depicts distress as turning invocation to Him.
Denies that beings apart from Allah control provision from heaven or earth.
Denies that those invoked apart from Allah can remove or redirect harm.
Shows all other invocations vanishing in sea danger, before people turn away after rescue.
Shows wealth and its owner abandoned without a party to help against Allah.
Rejects taking adversarial beings as protectors apart from Allah.
Exposes gods taken apart from Allah for imagined strength.
Shows those alleged gods rejecting their worshippers and turning against them.
Reassures Moses and Aaron that Allah is with them amid their threatened encounter.
Depicts disbelievers unable to repel the Fire from themselves and unable to be helped.
Questions who can protect people from Allah apart from Him.
Calls the invoked object a harmful protector and helper, a direct contrary example.
Challenges the assumption that Allah will not help His servant.
Promises Allah's help to those who support His cause and affirms His strength.
Denies that those facing punishment will receive help from Allah.
Contrasts Allah's sheltering power with the impossibility of sheltering against Him.
Denies that false gods possess harm, benefit, death, life, or resurrection.
Shows those invoked apart from Allah disclaiming power to avert punishment.
Denies benefit and harm to what is worshipped apart from Allah.
Names Allah as the responder to the distressed and remover of harm.
Denies provision from idols and directs provision-seeking and worship to Allah.
Denies any protector or helper apart from Allah.
Uses the fragile house of the spider as a parallel for taking protectors apart from Allah.
Denies intercessors among alleged partners at the moment those partnerships fail.
Denies any protector or intercessor apart from Allah.
Commands reliance on Allah and calls Him sufficient as guardian.
Places the confederate armies beside Allah's wind and unseen forces.
Shows Allah repelling the confederates while sparing believers from battle.
Denies that those invoked apart from Allah possess, share, or aid in dominion.
Limits intercession under Allah's authority, preventing it from functioning as independent rescue.
Makes divine mercy unwithholdable and unreleaseable by any other agent.
Denies that alleged partners possess even the smallest share of dominion.
Shows those invoked apart from Allah unable to hear, answer, or acknowledge the invocation.
Makes the holding of heavens and earth exclusive to Allah.
Names Allah as sufficient for His servant against the fear induced by others.
Denies that invoked partners can remove harm or withhold mercy decreed by Allah.
Returns all intercession to Allah's sole dominion.
Denies any protector from Allah on the day of turning away.
Promises divine help to messengers and believers in this life and at witness-bearing.
Denies protectors or helpers apart from Allah for those led astray.
Depicts the day when no protector can avail another and none are helped.
Calls invocation apart from Allah the furthest error because the invoked cannot answer.
Contrasts Allah's protection of believers with the disbelievers' lack of protector.
Names the promised outcome as mighty help from Allah.
Says that when the disbelievers fight, they will turn away and find neither protector nor helper.
Limits angelic intercession to Allah's permission and approval.
Exposes a promised alliance of aid as one that will not actually come through.
Qualifies the appearance of a united hostile force by describing divided hearts and defensive dependence.
Identifies Allah as owner of heaven and earth's stores, directly challenging claims of controlling provision.
Makes Allah the sole deity and directs believers to rely on Him.
States that whoever relies on Allah finds Him sufficient, alongside provision from unforeseen ways.
Names Allah as protector, with Gabriel, righteous believers, and angels as supporting forces.
Denies personal power over harm or right direction, keeping such control beyond human possession.
Denies any refuge or protector apart from Allah.
